title: Face with Bags Under Eyes Emoji 🫩: The Exhaustion Emoji
description: 🫩 is the newest tired face: heavy eye bags, flat mouth, no energy left. Learn what it says about burnout, bad sleep and being fed up, and how to use it.
summary: The 🫩 face with bags under eyes means exhausted, drained or completely over it. Approved in Unicode 16.0 in 2024, it filled a gap older tired emojis left open: none of them looked plainly worn out. It covers sleep deprivation, burnout, long shifts and the weary patience of dealing with something yet again.
meaning: Before this emoji existed, people who wanted to say they were tired had to choose between faces that were asleep, crying out or yawning. 🫩 shows the quieter kind of fatigue most adults actually feel: awake, functioning and running on nothing. The dark half-moons under the eyes do the talking, and the small flat mouth adds that there is no energy left even to complain.

It took off quickly because the look is so recognizable. Parents of newborns, students in exam season, nurses after a night shift and anyone on their fourth video call of the day found a face that matched. It is used literally for lack of sleep and loosely for emotional depletion, the feeling of having nothing more to give to a situation.

There is also a deadpan, fed-up reading. Sent in reply to an annoying message or a piece of news that is bad in a predictable way, 🫩 says I am too tired for this. It overlaps with the eye roll but without the attitude; the sender is not sneering, just spent. That dry, resigned humor is a large part of its appeal online.

Because it is recent, it does not show on older phones and operating systems. Recipients without support see an empty box or a question mark instead of the face, so the joke is lost on them entirely. It is worth knowing your audience before making it a habit, and falling back on 😩 or 😮‍💨 in group chats where devices vary.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: It answers the question how are you without any words. Friends send it on Monday mornings, after bad nights with a baby or a deadline, and at the end of a long week. It also works as a reply to someone else's exhausting story, as a form of solidarity.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: Among colleagues it is a mild, relatable way to admit you are stretched thin, especially after a launch or a run of late nights. It is honest without being alarming. With a manager it may invite a conversation about workload, which could be exactly what you want or not.

contexts.label: On TikTok and Instagram
contexts.body: Captions about burnout, parenting, shift work and chronic tiredness adopted it almost immediately. It also became a reaction to content that is draining to watch, such as a bad take or a long-running argument, where it means I do not have the strength for this today.

contexts.label: From a friend or partner
contexts.body: When someone close sends 🫩 with nothing else, they are usually asking for a little sympathy or patience rather than solutions. A kind reply, an offer to take something off their plate or simply a matching 🫩 is the expected response.

examples.meaning: A parent reporting a rough night and severe lack of sleep.
The sender is running on empty because of work or studying.

examples.text: He wants to circle back on it again 🫩
examples.meaning: Weary frustration at a tedious, repeated request.
A one-emoji answer: it is going exactly as badly as you would expect.

examples.text: Just landed after 14 hours 🫩 need a shower and a bed
examples.meaning: Travel fatigue after a long flight.

combos.meaning: Barely awake and relying on coffee to get through the morning.
Exhausted and falling apart, usually joked about during a stressful stretch.
Desperate for sleep and heading to bed as soon as possible.
Tired but pretending to be fine, with a clear note of sarcasm.

confusedWith.difference: 😫 is loud about its exhaustion, with scrunched eyes and a wailing mouth, and often expresses frustration. 🫩 is silent and flat. It shows the kind of tired that has stopped protesting.
😴 is asleep and at peace. 🫩 is the opposite problem: still awake when it should not be. Use 😴 for bedtime and 🫩 for the morning after too little of it.
😒 looks sideways in annoyance and blames someone. 🫩 can express being fed up too, but the cause is depletion rather than irritation, and it carries no accusation.

avoid: Do not rely on it with people who have older devices, since it may appear as a blank box.
Avoid sending it as your only reply to someone's exciting news; it can look like their happiness wears you out.
If you are seriously unwell or burned out, add words, because the emoji alone is easy to take as a joke.
design: A yellow face with half-lidded eyes, pronounced dark bags or creases beneath them and a short, flat or slightly downturned mouth. Vendors agree on the overall look, which follows the reference drawing closely. Some shade the bags in a darker orange-brown while others use simple curved lines, and the eyebrows may slope a little to add weariness.

faqs.a: Its official Unicode name is Face with Bags Under Eyes. People also call it the tired emoji, the exhausted emoji or the eye bags emoji. Searching any of those in an emoji keyboard on a supported device will usually bring it up.

faqs.q: Why can't I see the 🫩 emoji?
faqs.a: It was approved in Unicode 16.0 in 2024, and each company added it to its software on its own schedule after that. If your phone or computer has not been updated since, the character shows as an empty box. Updating the operating system normally fixes it.

No. Those two older faces are dramatic, with wide open mouths, and they are often used for whining, frustration or even excitement. 🫩 is specifically about fatigue and looks subdued. It was proposed because none of the existing options showed plain tiredness.

faqs.q: Does 🫩 mean someone is annoyed with me?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. It most often describes the sender's own state. If it arrives directly after something you asked for or said, it may mean your message added to their load, in a resigned rather than angry way. Asking is better than guessing.
